cim: Saudi artist combines artificial intelligence with traditional art

cim_eredeti: Saudi artist combines artificial intelligence with traditional art
szoveg_eredeti:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (MNTV) — Saudi artist Najla Al-Saleem is combining traditional painting with artificial intelligence-generated animations in her latest exhibition, A Shifting Horizon, bringing her own work and selected pieces by her late father, pioneering Saudi modernist Mohammed Al-Saleem, into an interactive artistic experience.

According to Arab News, the exhibition is running at Gallery Naila in Riyadh until November 19. Each displayed artwork is accompanied by a screen presenting a short animation generated using artificial intelligence, expanding on the original painting through movement and visual storytelling.

One of the exhibition’s central works is Composition No. 5, a collection of three colorful digital artworks created by Mohammed Al-Saleem on a computer in 1995. Najla believes the pieces were among the earliest digital artworks produced by a Saudi artist.

She considers the work particularly significant because it connects her father’s artistic experiments during the 1990s with contemporary digital creativity.

Mohammed Al-Saleem, who died in 1997, was an influential figure in Saudi Arabia’s modern art movement. He organized Riyadh’s first art exhibition in 1967 and established the city’s Saudi Art House in 1979.

He was particularly known for developing an artistic approach called “horizonism,” also referred to as the desert style, which became a defining feature of his work. Najla grew up observing her father develop the technique and later incorporated elements of it into her own artistic practice.

Horizonism generally places the main subject of a painting along a central horizon line, surrounded by expanding layers of color that move from darker to lighter shades. The compositions evoke desert landscapes, sand dunes and sunlight while also representing broader ideas about human aspirations and unattainable ambitions.

Najla has continued using this visual approach while extending its application beyond traditional desert imagery. She has incorporated architectural subjects, including traditional Najdi mud houses and contemporary buildings, into her compositions.

She explained that the desert style represents an atmosphere rather than requiring the literal depiction of desert landscapes, allowing artists to explore different subjects while retaining its underlying visual structure.

One example is her 2018 painting Jamsh, which adapts the horizonist technique by shifting attention toward the ground. The composition features mud buildings arranged across its central section, surrounded by contrasting bands of sand and coral colors.

The artist has described mud as an important material in Saudi cultural heritage, reflecting its historical role in traditional architecture and everyday life.

Artificial intelligence expands artistic possibilities

The decision to incorporate artificial intelligence into the exhibition originated with Najla, whose son, Tariq AlZaid, helped develop the animations through his company, LetsGoSky.

The process involved sessions in which the artist described the figures, subjects and visual elements within her paintings, providing the material needed to create short animated interpretations.

One of the examples is her 2012 painting Woman, which she associates with the movement for women’s rights in Saudi Arabia. The artwork depicts a dark, slender figure surrounded by radiating bands of yellow and orange.

In its animated version, the central figure begins moving and turning, with flowing arm movements that suggest freedom and self-expression.

Najla believes the use of artificial intelligence can introduce additional dimensions to static artworks by allowing audiences to experience their subjects through movement and alternative visual interpretations.

The gallery had previously experimented with similar technology during an exhibition dedicated to her father’s work, allowing visitors to scan QR codes and view selected paintings through animated digital presentations.

Tariq AlZaid described artificial intelligence as a tool that could produce positive or negative outcomes depending on how it was used. He said appropriate safeguards and approval mechanisms were necessary to ensure responsible implementation.

He also said the artwork’s data was stored within Saudi Arabia under the Kingdom’s data protection regulations and would not be used to train artificial intelligence models for other parties. According to him, ownership rights to the original artworks remained with the artists.

Exhibition manager Ameera AlZaben described the combination of Mohammed Al-Saleem’s pioneering artistic contributions and contemporary technology as an opportunity to connect different generations of artists.

She said the exhibition could provide younger creatives with an understanding of Saudi Arabia’s artistic history while encouraging them to experiment with emerging digital tools.

Najla has also emphasized the influence of her father’s willingness to explore unfamiliar artistic methods. He taught himself computer-based drawing and continued experimenting despite limited attention from critics.

She said his example had helped her approach new technologies and artistic possibilities with greater confidence, allowing her to continue developing the visual language he had established.

The exhibition brings together Saudi Arabia’s modern artistic heritage and contemporary digital experimentation, demonstrating how traditional visual styles can be reinterpreted through emerging technologies without abandoning their original cultural and artistic foundations.
